title: Ready to leave
hookLine: act, speak and think as one who could leave life at any moment (Meditations 2.11)

cards: Some people who travel for work keep a bag half packed. Toothbrush, charger, a clean shirt. When the call comes, they can be out the door in ten minutes, without panic, because nothing important is left undone.
In book two, Marcus writes himself a note about living like that. Not about wanting to go. About being the kind of person who could, without leaving a mess of unsaid things behind.

teach.h: YOU COULD LEAVE AT ANY MOMENT.
teach.b: First, the instruction. Section eleven begins: since you could leave life at any moment, let that shape every action, every word and every thought. It's not a threat.
It's an editing rule: if this might be the last thing I do, is this how I want to do it? Second, the reasoning. Marcus thinks out loud about what leaving means.

If there are gods, he says, departing isn't something to fear, because they wouldn't bring you into harm. If there were no gods, or they didn't care, why would he want to live in a world empty of them?
Then he says plainly what he believes: they do exist, and they do care. People today read that passage from many places: some share his faith, some don't, some aren't sure.

teach.h: HE REASONED HIS WAY TO CALM.
teach.b: All of them can notice that he reasoned his way to calm, not away from the question. Third, what isn't the point.

teach.h: THESE COME TO GOOD AND BAD ALIKE.
teach.b: Life and death, praise and blame, pain and pleasure, money and its lack, he says, happen to good and bad people alike, so they can't be what makes a life good or bad. What makes it good is how you live it. Fourth, ready.
Ready doesn't mean waiting to go, or wanting to.

teach.h: READY: NOTHING IMPORTANT LEFT FOR LATER.
teach.b: It means not leaving the important things for later: the apology, the thank you, the I love you you assume they know.
A traveler with a half-packed bag isn't hoping to leave. They're just free to live without dread. The entry points toward a fuller life, not a shorter one.

how: Some people who practice Stoicism use the thought of death as a prompt not to postpone what matters, such as apologies, thanks and time with people they love.

o: a rule for trimming long letters before sending them
letting life's shortness shape each act, word and thought
a law limiting what Roman writers could publish

games.q: ready to leave — tap the pairs.
p: let it shape every act and thought
Marcus believed they exist and care
come to good and bad alike

s: Marcus says to live as if you want to die soon
he says to live so that any moment could be the last and still be all right.
Marcus reasons through the case where there are no gods, then says he believes they exist and care
he faces the question and reasons his way to calm.
Marcus says pain and pleasure decide whether a life is good
they come to good and bad alike, so they can't.

games.q: you owe someone an apology. it's awkward, and there's always next week. what does Meditations 2.11 suggest?
o: do it today, as one who could leave at any time.
let it go; they've probably forgotten.
games.why: since you could leave life at any moment, Marcus says, let that shape every act, word and thought.

practice: This can feel heavy, so go gently. Think of one thing you'd regret leaving unsaid or undone, a thank you, an apology, a call to someone you love, and picture doing it simply, without drama. Notice how the day feels with it done.

wordCard.voice: Editing rule. Marcus's name for living as if you could leave life at any moment: let that shape every act, word and thought, and leave nothing important for later. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: ready. Not wanting to leave, just nothing important left for later. Day five hundred thirty-five, done.
